editorialPurpose: An adult medusa can reorganize through a cyst into polyps that bud new medusae; reversible development does not mean death is impossible.
storyAngle: Follow a change of body plan, then distinguish reversible development from invulnerability.

segments.text: What if an animal could reverse its own life cycle?
Normally, attached polyps bud off tiny jellyfish, which grow into swimming adults.
But injury or starvation can send an adult another way.
Its bell collapses. Its tentacles disappear. It settles into a cyst-like mass.
Inside, cells reorganize. Some can change their specialized identity: transdifferentiation.
A stolon grows, then polyps. That colony can bud new jellyfish.
Life-cycle reversal can happen repeatedly in laboratory cultures.
The molecular controls are still being studied.
But predators can still kill it. Reversal isn't guaranteed survival.
It doesn't make death impossible. It makes the direction of development reversible.

narrativeStructure.label: Impossible premise
narrativeStructure.purpose: One translucent species-informed adult medusa suspended in a dark teal water column, red-brown central manubrium, fine moving tentacles and grazing light. Immediate large subject and short curiosity statement.

narrativeStructure.label: Species identity
narrativeStructure.purpose: Stay with same adult. Camera arcs to reveal transparent bell and four radial canals; species name large enough to read. Original illustration disclosure.

narrativeStructure.label: Ordinary development
narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera descends to attached branching polyps. A pear-shaped medusa bud grows below a hydranth, detaches and rises; continue toward recognizable adult. No ephyra/disc stack.

narrativeStructure.label: A different route
narrativeStructure.purpose: Same adult loses pulse and descends toward substrate; tentacles retract and bell contracts. No clock, reversed footage, shrinking baby or injury gore.

narrativeStructure.label: Lose the medusa form
narrativeStructure.purpose: Continuous collapse toward a lobed intermediate then compact cyst-like mass on substrate. Bell and tentacles vanish as recognizable structures; time compression disclosed.

narrativeStructure.label: Reorganize
narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera pushes from surface of cyst into original illustrative tissue field; some elongated cells lose and change shape amongst surviving cells. No specific traced lineage, molecule, DNA repair visualization or literal microscopy. End by pulling toward cyst surface.

narrativeStructure.label: Grow a new body plan
narrativeStructure.purpose: A stolon visibly extends sideways from cyst. First polyp rises, then branches develop into a colony. A medusa bud subsequently detaches; support survives through sequence.

narrativeStructure.label: Repeatability
narrativeStructure.purpose: Widen to cultured colony/medusa relationship; restrained ghosted earlier stage chain indicates another possible reversal, not an infinite loop. Laboratory context explicit.

narrativeStructure.label: Known shape, open mechanism
narrativeStructure.purpose: Macro colony remains physical; briefly return to illustrative tissue field with varied cell identities. Molecular controls still studied; no identified master switch.

narrativeStructure.label: Survival has limits
narrativeStructure.purpose: Return to ocean scale: fragile medusa remains small against passing out-of-focus predator silhouette and light shadow. No specific predator species or escaping/resurrection performance implied.

narrativeStructure.label: The direction can change
narrativeStructure.purpose: Beautiful medusa above living attached polyp colony, then camera settles on colony and new bud ascending into light. Resolve initial adult-only mental model through changed developmental route; no infinity or guaranteed survival.
